extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students and researchers of British theatre and popular culture
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the defining features, history, performance conventions, venues, repertoire and social role of British music hall entertainment (mid-19th century to mid-20th century). Useful as a reference for understanding or reconstructing music-hall style performance and programming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / Core elements of music hall
rubrics_metrics.description: Music hall involved a mixture of popular songs, comedy, speciality acts, and variety entertainment; a form of British theatrical entertainment popular from the early Victorian era until around World War I (later rebranded as variety).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article repeatedly frames music hall as a hybrid entertainment form: song + supper rooms evolving into theatres offering a bill of varied acts (songs, comic acts, speciality performances). It notes overlap/analogy with North American vaudeville.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue form and audience arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Early music halls and purpose-built theatres were designed so audiences could eat, drink and smoke in the auditorium, with seating at tables and cheapest seats in the gallery — unlike conventional theatres with stalls and separate bar-rooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key venue features that define 'music hall' include table seating, integrated food/drink service, permissive auditorium behaviour. These features were later regulated away (e.g., ban on drinking in the auditorium) as respectability increased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical programme composition / bill structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Music-hall bills mixed vocal numbers (catchy popular songs) with comic turns and a wide range of speciality acts (acrobatics, magic, strongmen, animal acts, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers built shows from short, varied items to hold the attention of an often unruly urban audience; the programme relied on variety and frequent turn-taking rather than long-form drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song form and lyrical style
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical music-hall song consists of a series of verses sung by the performer alone and a repeated chorus carrying the principal melody, often encouraging audience participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects were contemporary, humorous, sentimental, patriotic or promotional (e.g., songs advertising alcoholic wares). Songs were designed to be catchy to engage jaded working-class urban audiences; many were written by professional songwriters rather than being traditional folk songs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience interaction and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences were mainly newly urbanised working-class people; participation (joining choruses, responsive behaviour) and familiarity with the situations sung about were expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The music-hall idiom developed to gain/hold attention of a 'jaded and unruly urban audience' — effective performances tailored content, pacing and chorus cues to encourage sing-alongs and direct audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer presentation and character types
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers typically dressed in character (or in eccentric styles) to suit their songs or sketches; stock performer types included lion comiques (toff characters), male/female impersonators, comic pianists and speciality artistes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts often relied on a strong stage persona and costume; performers like male impersonators could deliver social commentary. Original music-hall acts used minimal patter and focused on songs; later performers incorporated more developed sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music-hall comedy conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy ranged from sung narrative songs with little patter to sketch-based, physical humour (e.g., Fred Karno's 'speechless' sketches and visual gags such as the pie-in-the-face).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights Fred Karno's development of mime/sketch comedy without dialogue, the training ground this provided for figures like Chaplin and Laurel, and the centrality of physical and visual comedy forms in the tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speciality acts (spesh) taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Speciality acts encompassed a broad taxonomy including adagio (dance/juggling cross-acts), aerial acts, animal acts (talking dogs, flea circuses), cycling acts, strongmen, drag and impersonation acts, electric acts, escapologists, fire-eaters, jugglers/plate spinners, knife-throwing, magic, memory and mentalism acts, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These acts were integral to the variety of the bill; many evolved from circus forms. Examples and notable practitioners (e.g., Houdini, David Devant) are cited, indicating the wide range of spectacle expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural & production style of 'variety' palaces
rubrics_metrics.description: From the late 19th century the music-hall model evolved into ornate 'variety theatre' palaces with lavish exteriors, luxurious foyers and promenades, electric lighting and upmarket architectural design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transformation emphasized spectacle and respectability (architect, designer, decorator engaged), replacing earlier 'gaudy and tawdry' rooms; the promenade feature and tableaux vivants are cited as production/art direction elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation and licensing impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation and local licensing (Theatres Act 1843, London County Council restrictions, later bans on drinking in the auditorium) significantly affected where and how music-hall performances could be staged and contributed to changes in form and audience composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes how stricter licensing reduced numbers of small halls, how drinking bans altered auditorium culture, and how legal constraints prompted venues to adapt (e.g., reclassification as variety theatres or introduction of tableaux vivants to skirt rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural function and social role (including wartime)
rubrics_metrics.description: Music hall served social functions: popular entertainment for working-class urban communities, a site for patriotic mobilization (WWI recruitment songs and charity events), and a medium for social commentary and satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During WWI the halls staged recruitment and patriotic songs and charity shows; songs also reflected anxieties about changing gender roles. The article provides examples of recruitment songs and performers (Vesta Tilley, etc.) illustrating this public role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors contributing to decline and transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition from cinema, radio and recorded music, changing musical tastes (jazz, swing, big-band), television, changes in licensing (ban on drinking), and demographic shifts led to music hall's decline and its rebranding into 'variety' or disappearance by mid-20th century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page links concrete causes (technological competition, legal changes, cultural shifts) to the fading of many performers and venues; survival examples and derivative influences (stage/film musicals, TV recreations like The Good Old Days) are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repertoire and songwriting/production practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional songwriters were enlisted to meet demand for new catchy songs; tunes were sometimes repurposed (e.g., adoption of music-hall tunes by religious or other groups). The repertoire ranged from topical ditties to enduring hits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists numerous hit songs and their composers, indicating the commercial songwriting industry behind music hall and the importance of repeatable, transportable melodies and choruses for popularity and longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notions of respectability and commercialisation
rubrics_metrics.description: As the form matured, music hall navigated tensions between 'scandalous' popular entertainment and increasing respectability; syndicates and commercial circuits professionalized the industry, sometimes provoking labour disputes (e.g., Music Hall Strike of 1907).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article shows how commercialization (syndicates, circuits) and efforts to appeal to middle-class respectability changed programming, management practices, performer selection and even who was deemed acceptable for royal events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance casting and star-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful music-hall programming depended on star performers, memorable personas and repeatable hits; halls cultivated stars (Marie Lloyd, Dan Leno, George Formby) who could draw audiences and define the genre's public image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes the role of star performers and professional songwriters in establishing hits and the reliance of halls on recognizable names and signature numbers to sustain commercial viability.
